reviews.text: [b]EN[/b] wersja [b]PL[/b] poniżej [b]Playtime:[/b] 200+ hours [b]Status:[/b] Early Access [b]Recommendation:[/b] Absolutely yes After spending over 200 hours with Survival Machine, I can wholeheartedly recommend this title to anyone looking for a fresh take on the survival genre. This isn't just another game about collecting sticks in a forest — here, your home is a massive, moving machine traversing a procedurally generated world full of danger, resources, and challenges. The gameplay is based on a cyclical day-night structure. During the day, you explore and upgrade your base; at night, you defend it against waves of zombies. The crafting system is well-designed — intuitive despite being in Early Access, and reasonably deep, allowing you to create tools, weapons, traps, and fortifications, as well as upgrade both your character and your mobile fortress. Although the game offers co-op for up to four players, it's perfectly enjoyable solo. The gameplay is engaging, and the pacing can easily be adjusted to suit your preferred playstyle. The low-poly art style works brilliantly here — it’s clear, visually appealing, and gives the game a distinct atmosphere despite its post-apocalyptic setting. A major plus is the responsive and efficient technical support available on the official Discord. The developers are active, quick to respond to issues, and clearly committed to improving the game. Survival Machine stands out thanks to its originality, solid execution, and clear potential for something even greater. Even now, it offers many hours of satisfying gameplay and continues to evolve with each update. It's definitely worth a try. P.S. It’s worth kicking Paweł. :D [i]I was forced to disable comments because of how people have been acting lately. [/i] [hr][/hr] [b]Czas gry:[/b] 200+ godzin [b]Status:[/b] We wczesnym dostępie [b]Rekomendacja:[/b] Zdecydowanie tak Po ponad 200 godzinach spędzonych z Survival Machine mogę szczerze polecić ten tytuł każdemu, kto szuka świeżego podejścia do gatunku survival. To nie kolejna gra o zbieraniu patyków w lesie — tutaj Twoim domem jest wielka, poruszająca się maszyna przemierzająca proceduralnie generowany świat pełen zagrożeń, zasobów i wyzwań. Gra opiera się na cyklicznej strukturze dnia i nocy. W dzień eksplorujemy i rozwijamy bazę, w nocy bronimy się przed falami zombie. Crafting jest bardzo dobrze zaprojektowany — intuicyjny, mimo wczesnego dostępu jest w miarę rozbudowany, co pozwala na tworzenie narzędzi, broni, pułapek i umocnień oraz rozwój zarówno postaci, jak i mobilnej fortecy. Choć gra oferuje tryb współpracy do 4 graczy, spokojnie można grać solo i czerpać z tego pełną satysfakcję. Rozgrywka jest wciągająca, a tempo można dostosować do własnych preferencji. Grafika w stylu low poly sprawdza się tu znakomicie — jest czytelna, estetyczna i nadaje grze unikalny klimat, nawet mimo postapokaliptycznej scenerii. Na duży plus zasługuje także szybkie i sprawne wsparcie techniczne na oficjalnym Discordzie. Twórcy są aktywni, reagują na zgłoszenia i widać, że gra rozwija się w dobrym kierunku. Survival Machine wyróżnia się pomysłowością, solidnym wykonaniem i potencjałem na coś jeszcze większego. Już teraz oferuje wiele godzin dobrej zabawy i stale się rozwija. Zdecydowanie warto dać jej szansę. PS. Warto kopnąć Pawła. :D

Just some initial impressions: Nothing woke in the character creator. Simple, not that hard people ! The bones are here so far to be a great game. Original world. Playful Graphics. And a sense of humor. I accidentally got an achievement for kicking someone. Good laugh. The only negatives is I am not seeing a pause option for the massive audience of single players ( I have been told it does have it I just haven not noticed yet). And some of the quest language seems geared for multiplayer. Its a small gripe but would be nice to be able to imagine its a single player experience. Ran buttery smooth on my 4090 RTX. Shame that has to be pointed out but to many games with simple graphics run horrible these days. This does not. I will update after some hours of playtime.

怪物隨著日數越來越強, 只是藍圖科技都跟不上強度 然後一個人打就非常折磨 怪多起來一起砍你幾秒就死 但你得砍5~6刀 極度不推薦任何人去單人遊戲 最大缺點: 格擋判定很抽象 換工具會卡手 遠程武器的判定點是根據鏡頭的正中心位置, 所以當你鏡頭貼近牆壁的時候直接打不中 衝刺是屁用都沒有的 踢擊也是意義不明 體力條純粹搞笑 用劍的重擊速度過慢 甚至攻擊力比輕攻擊還低 後面有旋風式攻擊的鐵鏟喪屍 當他開始旋轉攻擊時是沒有任何攻擊判定 我直接被他極限反殺 當我看到艦上面有3隻以上的鐵鏟喪屍 我直接不用玩了 =========== Monsters scale ridiculously with each passing day, while your blueprints and techs struggles to keep up. Solo play is absolute torture – mobs can delete you in seconds, while you need 5-6 hits to kill one. Do yourself a favor and NEVER play this solo. The Biggest Issues: Blocking feels janky, and weapon swapping has awkward delay Ranged attacks only register from the EXACT center of your screen – kiss your shots goodbye if your camera clips into a wall Sprinting? Useless. Kicking? Pointless. Stamina bar? A bad joke Sword heavy attack is a complete joke: slower spins for 8+8 damage, while light attacks deal 10 per swing AND are faster Then come the nightmare shovel zombies with their broken spin attacks Their spinning hitbox is completely bugged – got reverse-ganked while I was wailing on one Spot 3+ shovel zombies in one area? Just quit and save yourself the frustration ======= Thanks for let me know coop part isn't what i expect it could work as it should be. So i deleted that part and let everyone know, they really need friends to play this game. ================================== New Update: They've fixed most of the single-player issues now, and the loot drops are even more generous. Honestly, I don't even need to craft anything at this point - I've got more equipment than I know what to do with! The developers also added a block icon for shovel zombies to indicate when they're immune to damage. Now, i need friends to play with, ha.

《Survival Machine》的世界里，人类文明又被丧尸攻陷了，现在剩下的只有我们的好友建造的这么一辆巨无霸战车，而这就是我们在这个丧尸遍地跑的世界里存活的依仗！ 在这里我们白天需要去探索、采集、战斗、收集各种资源，再利用这些资源制造成各种物品和设备，用以提升我们的巨无霸战车，让它从只能依靠我们人力防守变成一个移动的“丧尸噩梦”。当然，这自然是后话，在刚开始我们只能不断的武装自己，木棍、木剑、小弓箭这些虽然威力小点，但多轮几下也能干掉丧尸，谁让它们制作简单性价比高呢！至于后面的各种大杀器，那自然是后面生活滋润了才能解锁拥有的，那是后期的事了！！！那时候我们都能给我们的巨无霸战车布置各种大炮、弩炮等大杀器了！当然，为了应付夜晚那些个四处蜂拥而来的丧尸群，各种各样的陷阱也是效率很高的设备，多布置终究不会错的。 游戏除了各种制造和战斗之外，还有着一定的探索解谜元素，在这个世界里各处都藏有各种机缘和宝藏，想要获得自然需要开动我们的智力和操作，解谜能力高的可以轻松获得，差点的可能就会耽误不少时间了！（比如刚开始的锯木台蓝图，没有一定的观察力和逻辑思维，还真别想拿到）。 整体而言，《Survival Machine》虽然美术画面简单，但优化是相当的好，而且游戏内容相当丰富，白天探索收集建造，晚上防守战斗杀丧尸，还支持4人联机，有小伙伴一起玩那是相当酸爽，就是没有小伙伴，一个人也能玩得很舒服，相当值得推荐！ [quote]欢迎关注我们的鉴赏家:[url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/35402982/]走心评测[/url] ←遵从内心，写出真实感受 欢迎加入我们Steam组:[url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/ZXPC]走心评测[/url]←点击加入，一起探索游戏的乐趣 喜欢这篇评论，也麻烦点个赞，让更多人能够看到！[/quote]

Survival Machine: Mad Max Meets IKEA So I hopped into Survival Machine expecting chaos, cannibals, and a healthy dose of DIY doom-wagon driving. What I got was… well, all of that, plus a lot of accidentally falling off moving vehicles because I forgot physics exists. The game drops you into a desert with a janky contraption that looks like it was assembled by a raccoon with commitment issues. You gather stuff, upgrade your ramshackle ride, and desperately try not to be eaten while fending off bandits who were apparently trained at the Stormtrooper Academy of Terrible Aim. Pros: Build your very own post-apocalyptic clunker. It's like Pimp My Ride but everyone’s starving. Cons: Sometimes your biggest enemy isn’t the horde, it’s gravity. Or your own crewmates pushing you off ledges like it’s an accident. The AI occasionally forgets it's supposed to help you, not haunt you with thousand-yard stares. Final take: It's clunky, chaotic, and kinda dumb, but like, the fun kind of dumb. If you enjoy games where half the challenge is just keeping your weird contraption from flipping over like a drunk turtle, Survival Machine might be your jam.

The concept is great, the first few hours are fun, but after that, the gameplay becomes repetitive and frustrating. The machine you’re supposed to survive with becomes more of a burden than a feature. Needs refinement, especially in combat, performance, and meaningful progression. [h1] Gameplay [/h1] The central premise—surviving on a giant machine—is cool in theory, but the gameplay doesn’t live up to it. You don’t drive the machine or do anything significant with it; instead, it limits your movement. The map is generated around the machine, and straying too far resets you. The core gameplay loop gets stale fast: [list] [*]Visit all POIs [*]Loot chests [*]Collect mandatory resources and blueprints [*]Every X's night go back and defend the machine [*]Repeat [/list] The combat is [strike]♥♥♥♥[/strike] bad. Its bad. After a while enemies pile with abilities that are just annoying. Like one zombie can spin for an eternity and than you can kill him because he's just invincible while spinning. The difficulty also just scales the damage and that means that you need more resources for more weapons, because they break quickly. Blocking is also useless against multiple enemies. Tools are also like that: They break quickly, even the best you can craft. Every X's night you need to defend this giant piece of metal junk. You will build cannons as defense because they are the most effective. All other defenses have one ore more problems: awful targeting, no or too small AOE, or ridiculous reload times. The rewards for the mandatory quests are also stupid. ONE invisibility drink for 10 seconds? Why? [h1] Graphic & Music [/h1] Well, they are heavily stylized and look like 2000s. That wouldn’t be a problem if the game were well-optimized, but performance is rough. Also after playing the graphics are somewhat tone deaf, but maybe thats only a problem for me. As for the music - I can’t remember any of it, which says enough (played 5/6 weeks ago). [h1] Bugs [/h1] We didn’t run into major game-breaking bugs, but some issues are just stupid. [list] [*]Why don't have the lights on the machine collision?? You can even get up there via a ladder! [*]Most of the walls are just suggestions: You could bug yourself anywhere with enough patiance. [*]In last update I played at least the glitching through the machine was fixed... [/list] [h1] Story [/h1] None I guess? There is the element of "We need to survive" but I do not even know if your companion that gives you the quests WANT to survive. He's just too nonchalant about it all. Well maybe he know that there is no way to die and he could just ditch the stupid machine if bad comes to worse. Also: The machine is not explained in the slightest. It just does not make sense, there are no tracks for machines like that or any machine debris in the world. It looks like this machine is unique but it is just too gigantic for that. I just don't know how this machine fits in this western themed game. There are even railroad tracks, that are much more efficient to transport stuff. [h1] Coop [/h1] There are minor problems like lag and rubberbanding but nothing too broken. I would have played this game never, EVER alone. [h1] Final Thoughts [/h1] I don’t understand the “overwhelmingly positive” reviews. The concept is the only thing carrying this game. I would love to love this game because I love survival but it’s just not there. If you could [b]farm[/b] on the machine, or actually [b]drive[/b] it more, it would be awesome. But as it stands, it’s just a big useless base that restricts you. And there’s no real reason in the story for it to even exist. [b]Make the machine matter.[/b] Hopefully future updates will fix some of these core problems. If they do, I’ll gladly come back and update my review. Until then, I can’t recommend it.

I followed this game since when it was announced because of the intriguing premise: surviving on your moving settlement, like in Mortal Engines, while upgrading it and defending it against hordes of enemies. This, in theory. In practice, the game is middling for me at the moment (it's still in Early Access). Most of our time was spent gathering resources and clearing small obstacles while the SLOOOOOW giant machine with our base on it lumbered ahead in the background. When the promised zombie horde eventually attacked, it was... kind of lame and easily repelled by my pal and me, more an annoyance than a pulse-pounding moment. "Let's get rid of these losers and go back gather a hundred pieces of wood and rock to build another upgrade which... doesn't really do anything that interesting". Survival Machine is a neat concept, but it needs lots of improvement. Start by making the moving base faster and enemies deadlier - especially the horde attack, which was kind of a disappointment.

Great Game with a Lot of Potential Survival Machine is a very enjoyable game. The map is large and fun to explore, and the gameplay doesn’t feel too repetitive. There’s a good balance of zombies to keep things challenging, and resource gathering is satisfying — you can collect what you need without spending hours searching. That said, there are a few bugs. Sometimes your character may start floating out of nowhere. Thankfully, there’s an “Unstuck” button, but it teleports you all the way back to the machine, which can be frustrating. Other issues include the game randomly closing and problems when playing with others — specifically, getting stuck on the “Preparing Machine” screen when trying to load into multiplayer. Overall, despite the bugs, it’s a solid experience and worth checking out. I played it co-op and didn’t try the solo mode. The game has a clever idea: building a mobile machine that serves as your main base. It’s a concept that stands out from most survival games. The premise has a lot of potential, but in its current state, it needs much more work to feel polished and enjoyable. The early hours I felt the urge to explore the world and experience traveling with the machine. However, progression quickly becomes all about repetitive crafting. Almost every main quest requires crafting new tools and items from start to finish, which makes the pacing slow and sometimes tedious. This could’ve easily been simplified or front-loaded in the first hour instead of forming the backbone of the entire quest structure. Crafting is the core of the experience, but it feels limited and lacks depth. A simple repair system for tools and weapons would help a lot instead of forcing players to rebuild everything, especially since resources aren’t always easy to find. Player movement, controls, and combat all need improvement. Activities, environments, and even bosses repeat often. Facing the same boss multiple times gets dull, and important areas lack meaningful challenges, such as adding unique bosses that could have encouraged exploration and balanced risk versus reward. I don't recommend the game in its current state, but I still believe the idea itself deserves more development. It has a unique core that could turn into something great if it gets the attention it needs.

Voice acting is a bit weird and awkward. Looks like the dev (there's a 'team' sorta, but it looks like really it's mostly one dev) has a crush he can't get past costing his team(?) real actual dollars. Ah, youth. Other than that, it's an open world that... isn't. I couldn't put my finger on why such a pretty handcrafted place didn't click at all, but it finally dawned on me. I've played dozens of games where you go out and explore and find and return, loot in hand. One of the exciting portions of this is to see WHAT you can find, and the excitement of getting something new/different/useful. In Survival Machine, you're just obligated to get some item that you HAVE to get to progress. And that progression limits any feeling of exploration, which would be the charm of this game. You can't move your 'base' such as it is; there's no feeling of freedom whatsoever. It's literally on rails. Imagine Valheim, or Satisfactory, or Icarus, or pick-literally-any-successful-base-builder - and those games released with ONE area you could build a base in, in the ENTIRE friggin' map. They'd get rip to shreds. Horrible, people would say. And rightly so. Survival machine embraces this wholeheartedly, for some reason, and solves the treadmill problem by putting your static base location on unmoving rails. There's no player decision making, at all, whatsoever. Not one single iota. Nothing you think matters, or choose. It's all just one *very* long fetch quest. There's some other psychological elements too, that maybe feel like design decisions or the (quite sensitive) dev may brush off as being 'not the player's cup of tea' but are actually just portions of human psychology they decided to ignore/not understand: If you can move faster than an object, and that object also moves slower than you can in *real life*, players would feel agonizingly constrained by it. Consider this: one game, you play as an amoebic slime, gathering food in your petri dish. You watch your slime crawl across the screen at 0.0000001m/s for a solid MINUTE. Game refunded, 1000%. Now, second game - you fly in your spaceship, at warp speed, flitting across the galaxy. You warp across an ENTIRE STAR SYSTEM for your next planet/asteroid to mine. You're burning at high speed for a solid MINUTE. Whew, those engines are running hot! Exciting experience! Functionally, these are the same tasks to game code, with a different veneer and psychology to them. You could be walking through a room, or sprinting through a house. Players will hate you if you don't have a sprint key, even if your game isn't scaled for, or meant to have, a sprint key. Similarly, if you're always running back to some crawling, lumbering behemoth, even if YOU think it's cool, you're fighting against basic human psychology.

Survival Machine takes a familiar zombie survival formula and gives it a refreshing twist by placing players aboard a massive mobile fortress instead of a traditional stationary base. Developed by Grapes Pickers and published by Games Operators and PlayWay S.A., the game combines exploration, crafting, construction, and cooperative gameplay into an experience centered around keeping a colossal machine moving through a dangerous post-apocalyptic landscape. This innovative concept immediately sets it apart from many survival games, as progress depends not only on gathering resources but also on constantly advancing into unexplored territory while ensuring the machine remains operational and well defended. The gameplay follows a satisfying day-and-night cycle that keeps players engaged with changing priorities. Daylight hours are dedicated to venturing into the surrounding wilderness in search of valuable resources, crafting materials, food, and equipment. Every expedition presents opportunities to discover new locations and gather the supplies needed to improve the fortress. Once night falls, however, the focus shifts dramatically as waves of zombies descend upon the machine. These nightly assaults create tense defensive encounters that reward players who spent their daytime preparing effective fortifications and stockpiling the right resources. This balance between exploration and defense gives the game a steady rhythm that rarely feels repetitive. The game's mobile base is easily its defining feature. Rather than constructing a permanent settlement, players continuously upgrade a moving fortress that acts as transportation, shelter, workshop, and defensive structure all at once. New crafting stations, storage facilities, protective walls, weapons, and specialized modules gradually transform the humble machine into an impressive armored stronghold capable of surviving increasingly dangerous threats. Every improvement has a practical purpose, making progression feel rewarding while reinforcing the importance of careful planning and resource management. Crafting and building systems offer considerable flexibility, encouraging players to customize the machine according to their preferred playstyle. Resource collection remains meaningful throughout the adventure because every new biome introduces materials necessary for advanced technologies and upgrades. Deciding which improvements deserve priority becomes an engaging strategic element, especially when resources are limited. The sense of watching the fortress evolve from a vulnerable vehicle into a heavily fortified mobile headquarters provides a constant feeling of accomplishment throughout the campaign. Combat is straightforward but effective, emphasizing preparation rather than mindless action. Players can fight zombies directly using crafted weapons or allow carefully designed defenses to absorb much of the pressure during nighttime attacks. Positioning barricades, reinforcing weak points, and upgrading equipment all contribute to surviving the growing difficulty. While the enemy variety may not be extensive compared to some established survival games, the increasing intensity of the attacks keeps players alert and reinforces the importance of long-term planning instead of relying solely on combat skills. Cooperative multiplayer significantly enhances the overall experience. Supporting up to four players, Survival Machine encourages teamwork by allowing each participant to take on different responsibilities. One player may focus on harvesting resources, another on expanding the machine, while others handle crafting, exploration, or defending against incoming zombie hordes. This natural division of labor creates satisfying cooperative moments where communication and coordination directly influence success. Although the game remains playable solo, its mechanics clearly feel designed to shine when shared with friends. Visually, the game embraces a colorful stylized art direction rather than pursuing gritty realism. The bright environments, appealing low-poly visuals, and varied landscapes create an inviting atmosphere that contrasts nicely with the zombie-infested setting. Different regions introduce fresh scenery that keeps exploration visually interesting, while the clean presentation helps players easily identify resources, structures, and approaching enemies. Although the graphics prioritize style over technical realism, they complement the gameplay well and contribute to the game's accessible personality. As an evolving title, Survival Machine still has room for growth. Some systems could benefit from additional depth, greater enemy diversity, and expanded late-game content to improve long-term replay value. Certain mechanics may also require further balancing and refinement as development continues. Fortunately, the core concept is already strong enough to support future updates, and the developers have established a solid framework that can be expanded with additional content over time. Survival Machine succeeds because it introduces a genuinely creative idea into a genre crowded with similar experiences. The moving fortress transforms the usual survival gameplay loop into something more dynamic by combining exploration, base building, crafting, and defense into one interconnected system. Supported by enjoyable cooperative play, satisfying progression, and an engaging cycle of preparation and survival, the game offers a memorable adventure for players who enjoy building, scavenging, and overcoming challenges with friends. While there is still room for further refinement, its originality and strong gameplay foundation make it an easy recommendation for fans of cooperative survival games. Rating: 7/10

I just finished the game this evening, clocking in at 67 hours. I played it exclusively solo. It has just enough pros to outweigh the cons to me, so I'll do a rundown. Great: - responsive devs who understand that not everyone likes Discord. They responded to posts in the Steam forums in a timely fashion, and, one of the bugs I found (also noticed by others), was patched within a few days. That's good effort. Good: + Nice music, and I love the little gramophones you can find to play little snippets of songs I'd like to see expanded into full-length songs. + Runs great on my decent, but not "top-class" rig + unexpected automation options available later on, though simple, were appreciated + decent variety of simple puzzles. My favorite was the cemetery with its small-scale "pay attention and LOOK around" style of information gathering to solve it. + We're rolling on a giant, slow train machine that we can build on, pretty cool + Generally rewarding resource collection. You get a decent amount of resources from busting one rock or one tree, not one or two "wood" or "stone" + automated turrets. I love turrets, mines, traps, automated defenses, etc., in almost any game. I find few combat experiences more satisfying than not lifting a finger and watching my "wall o' death" take care of intruders. + vertical building. You can build multiple levels on your survival machine. I ended up with a ground layer for defense and primary workstations, a secondary level for energy production and lesser used workstations, and a third level for a private house/storage. Cons: - the game definitely seems marketed more toward children. You get farting zombies, silly zombie sounds, zombies with pails on their heads, and a villain that, while adequately voiced, sounds like he's been told he's a villain in a game for seven year olds. "You've not seen the last of meeeeee!", maniacal (yet not too scary) laughter, "Wait until you see my ultimate weapon!", etc. I ended up muting the game whenever Zombieburg *sigh* showed up. - only two biomes. While they differ quite a bit and are well designed overall, I was disappointed that we didn't get a bit more variety. - Some of the puzzle rewards are really underwhelming (a handful of flowers and a few planks?). I stopped doing most of them after I realized that you could usually just advance the train to a new spot if you didn't find an "easy" lootbox to get the recipe you needed. - irritating "snowstorm" mechanic in the alpine region. Overall, I had a good time with the game. It's not something I would be likely to replay again, but when I wanted a more light-hearted gaming experience than what I usually play, it came along at the right time.

[h2]Mortal Engines From Temu in a Low-Poly Zombie Apocalypse[/h2] As the title suggests, the first thing that crossed my mind when looking at Survival Machine’s premise was Mortal Engines; a voluminous dieselpunk novel, later adapted into a (rather rushed) movie; a tale of enormous, moving machine-city-states that scavenge for resources and, in some cases, prey on each other. The idea of building, maintaining and upgrading my own, custom miniature ‘mortal engine’ while roaming a zombie-infested, post-apocalyptic world sounded promising, even if I wouldn’t be building a whole city, but rather a single house at best, nor be put against other ones in battle. Hence, the ‘Temu’ part; as in, a scaled-down, knockoff version of that baseline idea, that still remains a good concept unto itself, although not exactly novel. That premise was in part concretized as I roamed the wastes, progressively arming, expanding and fortifying my base to survive the zombie threat every few nights; however, it was also driven back by annoying bugs, a few questionable design choices and, above all, a lackluster challenge level even on the hardest setting available. Survival Machine is a competent open-world crafting title, but is significantly drawn back by a plethora of questionable design choices, balance issues and annoying bugs. Its foundation is solid; however, the execution lacks the polishing and refinement you’d expect from a full release. I would say that this game plays out more like a beta-stage than a fully finished title, even for indie standards. I’d still recommend it to fans of base building-heavy titles that don’t mind some repetitive grinding, and to any who enjoy tower defense and efficient organization of base layouts. I think people are really harsh with this game. This is an indie game that costs ~15€. For this price you get: - a functioning moving base that you defend once every 2 to 3 nights from waves of zombies. - A semi open world with a good amount of poi diversity that are resolved using little simple jumping puzzles and/or fighting off the zombies - a fun little story, nothing too complex but not boring in itself - specific map unique poi that require you to complete a certain number of steps to open the way for your machine (blow up a fortress, open some massive doors...) I just finished the first biome and I got to say the game is fine. I didn't have any connectivity issues and minimal bugs, nothing game breaking. This is a 15€ game from a dev that obviously cares a lot by the amount of reviews he has answered here. Sure there are better games and there are worst games. This is a good game and I'm having fun.
